questionText: Table students (id PRIMARY KEY, name, email, city, age) with 1,000,000 rows. Only the primary key exists. What does MySQL do for SELECT * FROM students WHERE email = 'zoya@mail.com'?
option1: Jumps straight to the row, because MySQL automatically indexes every column of a table
option2: Reads every row and checks its email, because nothing in the table is sorted by email (full table scan)
option3: Uses the primary key tree to find the email, because that tree keeps every column in sorted order
option4: Looks the email up in the buffer pool, which keeps a sorted list of all emails in memory
correctOptionExplanation: The primary key tree is sorted by id only. With no index on email, the only way is to check every row.

questionText: Table students (id PRIMARY KEY, name, email, city, age) with 1,000,000 rows. What does MySQL do for SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 500000?
option1: Walks the primary key B+ tree from the root down to one leaf, reading only a handful of pages
option2: Reads every row from the start, because an id is just another column in the table
option3: Reads a secondary index first, then follows its pointer to the primary key of the row
option4: Reads rows in the order they were inserted until it reaches the one with that id
correctOptionExplanation: The table is stored in a B+ tree sorted by id, so finding one id means going down one path from root to leaf.

questionText: Table students (id PRIMARY KEY, name, email, city, age) with 1,000,000 rows. After CREATE INDEX idx_email ON students(email), how does SELECT * ... WHERE email = 'zoya@mail.com' run?
option1: It reads idx_email only, because a secondary index stores the full row in its leaves
option2: It finds the id in idx_email, then fetches the row from the primary key tree
option3: It still reads every row, but faster, because the index tells MySQL to skip empty pages
option4: It searches the primary key tree directly, because idx_email has re-sorted the table by email
correctOptionExplanation: A secondary index lookup is two steps in InnoDB: the email index gives the id, and the id leads into the clustered (primary key) tree for the rest of the row.

questionText: In InnoDB, what does a leaf of the secondary index idx_email hold?
option1: A complete copy of the row, so the table never has to be read again
option2: The physical disk address of the row, so MySQL can jump straight to it
option3: Only the email values in sorted order, with no link back to the row
option4: The email value plus the primary key (id) of the row it belongs to
correctOptionExplanation: Secondary indexes point to rows through the primary key value, not a disk address. That is why a full-row lookup needs a second trip into the primary key tree.

questionText: What is the clustered index of an InnoDB table?
option1: Any index created with CREATE INDEX, because it groups rows that share the same value together
option2: A separate copy of the table, sorted by whichever column is queried most often
option3: An index on a column with few distinct values, which groups the rows into clusters
option4: The primary key tree itself, whose leaves hold the full rows in key order
correctOptionExplanation: In InnoDB the table is the primary key tree. Every other index is a non-clustered (secondary) index that points back to it.

questionText: How many clustered indexes can one InnoDB table have, and why?
option1: One per column, because every column can sort the rows in its own way
option2: Two: the primary key and one UNIQUE index chosen when the table is created
option3: None, unless the index is declared with the CLUSTERED keyword in CREATE INDEX
option4: Exactly one, because the rows themselves can be physically stored in only one order
correctOptionExplanation: The clustered index decides where the rows live. Data can only be arranged one way, so there can only be one; all other indexes are secondary.

questionText: An InnoDB table is created without a primary key. What does InnoDB do?
option1: It clusters by the first UNIQUE NOT NULL index, or else by a hidden row id
option2: It refuses to create the table, because every InnoDB table must declare a primary key
option3: It stores the rows as an unsorted pile, with no tree at all, until a key is added
option4: It makes every column a clustered index, so that any lookup can find the row directly
correctOptionExplanation: InnoDB always needs a clustered index. Declaring your own short primary key is better, because a hidden id cannot be used in your queries.

questionText: Why is a random UUID usually a worse primary key than an auto-increment id in InnoDB?
option1: UUIDs cannot be indexed at all, so every lookup by primary key becomes a full table scan
option2: Auto-increment ids are stored in memory only, so they are always faster than anything on disk
option3: A UUID primary key turns the table into a heap, so the clustered index is lost completely
option4: Inserts scatter across random pages, and every secondary index stores the bigger key
correctOptionExplanation: With increasing ids, new rows are appended at the right edge of the tree. Random keys scatter inserts across the tree, and because secondary indexes store the primary key, a 16-byte key makes them all bigger.

questionText: Table marks has PRIMARY KEY (class, roll_no), so rows are sorted by class first, then roll_no. How does WHERE class = 10 AND roll_no = 7 run?
option1: A full scan, because a composite key can only be searched one column at a time
option2: A lookup on roll_no first, then a scan of every class to find class 10
option3: A normal tree lookup: go down to class 10, then to roll 7 within it
option4: Two separate lookups, one per column, whose results are joined afterwards
correctOptionExplanation: Both columns of the key are given, so the tree can be followed exactly like a single-column key.

questionText: Table marks has PRIMARY KEY (class, roll_no), so rows are sorted by class first, then roll_no. How does WHERE roll_no = 7 run?
option1: A tree lookup, because roll_no is part of the primary key and every key column is searchable
option2: A lookup on the last class only, because roll numbers are unique across the whole school
option3: A full scan: roll 7 exists inside every class, so the sort order on class does not help
option4: An error, because a query must mention the first column of the primary key
correctOptionExplanation: The tree is sorted by class first. Without a class, MySQL has no place to jump to; the roll-7 rows are spread across all classes.

questionText: Table marks has PRIMARY KEY (class, roll_no), so rows are sorted by class first, then roll_no. How does WHERE class = 10 run?
option1: It jumps to the first class-10 row, then walks the leaves until the class changes
option2: A full scan, because only the full key (class and roll_no together) can be used
option3: It reads only one row, because the tree stops at the first match of the first column
option4: It reads the whole table backwards until it reaches the first class-10 row
correctOptionExplanation: This is the leftmost-prefix rule: using only the first column of a composite key still lets MySQL jump in, then read a continuous stretch of leaves.

questionText: Index idx_city_age on students(city, age). How does WHERE age = 30 run?
option1: It uses the index exactly like WHERE city = 'Pune', because both columns are in the index
option2: It usually cannot use the index to jump in, because rows with age 30 are spread across every city
option3: It uses the index, because MySQL reads composite indexes from the last column backwards
option4: It fails with an error, because age is not the first column of any index on the table
correctOptionExplanation: The index is sorted by city first. Skipping the first column is like looking up a surname-first phone book by first name only. (MySQL 8 can sometimes do a "skip scan" when the first column has very few values, but do not design around it.)

questionText: Index idx_city_age on students(city, age). How does SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = 'Pune' ORDER BY age run?
option1: It finds the Pune rows with the index, then sorts them by age in memory afterwards
option2: It finds the Pune entries and reads them already sorted by age, so no extra sort is needed
option3: It scans the whole table, because ORDER BY always forces MySQL to ignore indexes
option4: It sorts all one million rows by age first, then picks out the ones from Pune
correctOptionExplanation: Inside one city the index is already ordered by age, so the ORDER BY comes for free. EXPLAIN shows no "Using filesort".

questionText: A hot query is WHERE city = 'Pune' AND age > 25. Which index serves it best?
option1: (age, city): the range column first, so that MySQL can skip the young students quickly
option2: Two separate indexes, one on city and one on age, which are always better than one composite
option3: (city, age): the equality column first lets MySQL jump to Pune, then read the age range in order
option4: An index on age alone, because ranges are the expensive part of every query
correctOptionExplanation: Rule of thumb: equality columns first, the range column last. With (city, age) the Pune rows with age over 25 sit together in one stretch of the index.

questionText: Index idx_age_city on students(age, city). Why is it a weak fit for WHERE age > 25 AND city = 'Pune'?
option1: It is not weak: column order inside a composite index never changes how a query runs
option2: MySQL cannot use any index at all when a query mixes a range with an equality
option3: The index works, but only if the WHERE clause is rewritten as city = 'Pune' AND age > 25
option4: The range on age comes first, so the Pune entries are scattered and city is checked one by one
correctOptionExplanation: After a range, the entries for the next column are no longer in one block: Pune students are scattered across all ages above 25. Put the equality column first.

questionText: Two filters are always used together as equalities: WHERE city = ? AND age = ?. How do you pick the column order of a composite index?
option1: Always put the column with the longer name first, because MySQL compares names to pick the index
option2: Either order works for this query; pick the one that also helps your other queries most
option3: Always put age first, because numbers are compared faster than strings inside an index
option4: The order must match the order of the conditions in the WHERE clause, or the index is ignored
correctOptionExplanation: With two equalities both orders find the rows directly. The tie-breaker is the leftmost rule for your other queries.

questionText: An app shows a user's order history: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Which index fits?
option1: (created_at, user_id): sort everything by date first, then look for user 42 in that order
option2: (user_id, created_at): jump to user 42, whose orders are already in date order, and read just 20
option3: An index on created_at only, because ORDER BY is the slowest part of the query
option4: An index on status, because order history pages usually show the status of each order
correctOptionExplanation: Equality (user_id) first, then the ORDER BY column. MySQL reads the newest 20 entries for that user and stops.

questionText: A flash-sale page runs WHERE category = 'shoes' AND price < 1000. Which index fits?
option1: (category, price): jump to shoes, then read the prices below 1000 in one continuous stretch
option2: (price, category): read every cheap product first, then keep only the shoes
option3: An index on price only, because every flash sale filters on price before anything else
option4: No index: a flash sale only lasts a few hours, so the table is scanned during that time
correctOptionExplanation: Equality first, range last again. A sale page is hit by many users at once, so this query is worth an index.

questionText: Users log in with WHERE email = ?, and two accounts must never share an email. What should you create?
option1: A UNIQUE index on email: it makes the login lookup fast and rejects duplicate emails
option2: A normal index on email, plus a SELECT before every insert to check for duplicates
option3: Nothing: the primary key already guarantees that every column of a row is unique
option4: An index on (email, password), so that the login check is covered by the index
correctOptionExplanation: A UNIQUE index is a B+ tree like any other, with one extra rule: it refuses a second row with the same value. One structure gives both speed and correctness.

questionText: Query: SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN users u ON o.user_id = u.id WHERE u.id = 42. Which index matters most for the join?
option1: An index on users.id, because the primary key of users is not indexed by default
option2: An index on orders.user_id, so MySQL visits only user 42's orders instead of all of them
option3: An index on orders.id, because joins always go through the primary keys of both tables
option4: No index: joins are done in memory, so indexes on joined columns are never used
correctOptionExplanation: users.id is already the primary key. The side that needs help is orders, filtered by user_id; InnoDB also creates this index for you when you declare a foreign key.

questionText: Products need a search box: "find products whose description contains wireless". What fits?
option1: A normal index on description, because LIKE '%wireless%' can then jump straight to the rows
option2: A composite index on (description, name), so the search can use the leftmost column
option3: A UNIQUE index on description, so each word appears only once in the table
option4: A FULLTEXT index or a search engine, since a B+ tree cannot search inside text
correctOptionExplanation: A B+ tree is sorted from the first character, so "contains" gives it nowhere to start. Full-text indexes are built by word for exactly this.

questionText: Which query can use an index on students(name)?
option1: WHERE name LIKE 'Zo%', because names starting with Zo sit together in the sorted index
option2: WHERE name LIKE '%ya', because the index stores every name, including its ending
option3: WHERE name LIKE '%oy%', because LIKE with two wildcards triggers a special index search
option4: All three of these, because LIKE always uses an index when one exists on the column
correctOptionExplanation: A known start of the string lets MySQL jump in and read a range. A leading % means the matches can be anywhere in the sorted order.

questionText: Column is_active is true for 95% of users. Is an index on is_active a good idea for WHERE is_active = true?
option1: Yes, because any column used in a WHERE clause should always have its own index
option2: Yes, because a column with only two values makes the smallest and therefore fastest index
option3: Usually not: most rows match, so a scan is cheaper than the index
option4: No, because MySQL is not able to create an index on a boolean column
correctOptionExplanation: An index pays off when it narrows the search to a few rows. When nearly everything matches, every match costs an extra trip into the primary key tree.

questionText: Orders has an index on status. 90% of orders are DELIVERED. For WHERE status = 'DELIVERED', EXPLAIN shows a full table scan. Why?
option1: The index is broken and must be rebuilt, because MySQL always uses an index when one exists
option2: MySQL never uses an index for text values, only for numbers and dates
option3: The query is missing ORDER BY status, which is required before the index can be used
option4: Most rows match, so reading the table in order beats one index lookup per row
correctOptionExplanation: The optimizer estimates the cost of both plans. For a value that matches most rows, the scan wins.

questionText: Same orders table and index. WHERE status = 'REFUND_PENDING' matches only a few rows. What happens now?
option1: MySQL uses the status index, because this value narrows the search down to a few rows
option2: It still scans the table, because the optimizer decides once per index, not per query value
option3: It scans the table, because the index was skipped for DELIVERED in the earlier query
option4: It uses the primary key tree, because the status index only stores DELIVERED orders
correctOptionExplanation: Same index, different value, different plan. The decision depends on how many rows are expected to match (selectivity).

questionText: A lookup table of 30 countries has an index on name, but EXPLAIN shows a full scan for WHERE name = 'India'. Should you worry?
option1: No: the whole table is a page or two, so a scan costs about the same
option2: Yes: the index is corrupt, because a small table should always use its indexes
option3: Yes: every query must show an index in EXPLAIN, or it will not scale later
option4: No: small tables are kept in a different storage engine that has no indexes
correctOptionExplanation: Indexes matter when tables are large. For a tiny table, a scan touches the same handful of pages.

questionText: orders has an index on created_at. Why can WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025 not use it to jump in?
option1: YEAR() only works on unindexed columns, so MySQL drops the index whenever it is used
option2: Dates are stored as text in the index, so year comparisons always need a full scan
option3: The index is sorted by created_at, not by YEAR(created_at), so it cannot jump in
option4: It can use it: functions are applied to the index entries before the search starts
correctOptionExplanation: Rewrite it as a range on the bare column: created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-01'. Now the index can jump to the start of 2025.

questionText: students has idx_email, and emails are stored as typed by users. Why does WHERE LOWER(email) = 'zoya@mail.com' not use the index?
option1: LOWER() makes the comparison case-insensitive, and case-insensitive searches can never use an index
option2: The index holds the emails as they were stored, not their lowercase version
option3: Indexes on email columns are only used for UNIQUE checks, not for searching
option4: It does use the index, because MySQL lowercases every index entry automatically
correctOptionExplanation: Fix it in the data: store emails lowercased and compare against a lowercased value. (MySQL 8 can also index an expression with a functional index.)

questionText: Column phone is VARCHAR and indexed. Why does WHERE phone = 9876543210 (no quotes) end up scanning the table?
option1: Numbers longer than nine digits are too big to be stored in an index
option2: Comparing text with a number converts every phone first, so the index is skipped
option3: Phone columns are never indexed by MySQL, whatever their type
option4: The query works the same; the scan is caused by something else in the table
correctOptionExplanation: Match the type of the column: WHERE phone = '9876543210'. A type mismatch silently turns a fast lookup into a full scan.

questionText: products has an index on price. Why does WHERE price * 1.18 > 1000 scan the table, and what is the fix?
option1: Multiplication is not allowed in a WHERE clause on an indexed column; remove the index
option2: Decimal prices cannot be indexed; store prices as text so they can be indexed
option3: The math is done on the column; rewrite it as price > 1000 / 1.18
option4: Comparisons with > never use an index; change the query to use = instead
correctOptionExplanation: Keep the indexed column bare on one side of the comparison. Then MySQL can jump to the right place in the sorted index.

questionText: Only city has an index. How is WHERE city = 'Pune' OR age = 30 likely to run?
option1: With the city index alone, because OR only needs the first condition to be indexed
option2: With the city index for Pune, then the rest of the table is skipped as already checked
option3: With the primary key tree, because OR queries always switch to the clustered index
option4: As a full scan: rows with age 30 can be anywhere, and there is no index to find them
correctOptionExplanation: With OR, every age-30 row must be found too. If both columns had their own index, MySQL could combine them (index merge) or you could split the query with UNION.

questionText: A product listing runs SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE category = 'shoes'. With an index on (category, name, price), what is special about this query?
option1: It must still read each full row, because SELECT always fetches rows from the clustered index
option2: It cannot use the index, because name and price are not the leftmost columns
option3: It runs slower, because a three-column index is too large to search efficiently
option4: It is answered from the index alone, with no trip to the table for any row
correctOptionExplanation: This is a covering index: EXPLAIN shows "Using index". Avoiding the second lookup per row is what makes it fast.

questionText: students has idx_email. Why can SELECT id, email FROM students WHERE email = ? skip the trip into the primary key tree?
option1: Because id is the primary key, MySQL always returns it without reading anything
option2: Because selecting fewer columns makes MySQL skip every index and read the table directly
option3: It cannot skip it: a secondary index lookup always needs the primary key tree too
option4: Each idx_email leaf already holds both the email and the id, so the index covers it
correctOptionExplanation: In InnoDB every secondary index carries the primary key, so queries that need only the indexed columns plus the id are covered.

questionText: A table has 6 indexes. What does each INSERT now cost compared with having only the primary key?
option1: Nothing extra: indexes are rebuilt in the background once a day
option2: Only one extra write, because all secondary indexes share a single tree
option3: The row goes into the primary key tree and into all 6 index trees
option4: Less, because indexes tell MySQL where the new row should go
correctOptionExplanation: Every index is its own B+ tree that must stay sorted. More indexes = faster reads for those queries, but slower writes and more disk.

questionText: An event-logging table receives 50,000 inserts per second and is rarely read. How many secondary indexes should it have?
option1: One on every column, so that any future query is already fast
option2: Many, because indexes speed up inserts by telling MySQL where to place each row
option3: Exactly one per column used in the INSERT statement, to keep inserts sorted
option4: As few as possible, ideally none, since each one slows every insert
correctOptionExplanation: Index for the reads you actually run. A write-heavy table that is rarely queried pays the cost of every index and gets little back.

questionText: A table has an index on (city) and another on (city, age). What can usually be done?
option1: Drop (city): the (city, age) index already serves queries on city alone
option2: Drop (city, age): two columns in one index are always slower than a single column
option3: Keep both: MySQL needs a single-column index before it can use a composite one
option4: Merge them into (age, city), which serves every query the two indexes served
correctOptionExplanation: Leftmost rule again: (city, age) can be used for city alone. A redundant index still costs a write on every insert.

questionText: You run CREATE INDEX idx_email ON students(email) on a table that already has 10 million rows. What happens?
option1: It finishes instantly, because the index is filled lazily the first time a query uses it
option2: Only new rows are indexed; old rows stay unindexed until they are updated
option3: MySQL reads every existing row to build the tree, which takes time
option4: The table is copied into a new clustered index sorted by email
correctOptionExplanation: An index must contain every row from the start, so building it means reading the whole table once. Plan it like any big data change.

questionText: Where do index pages live, and what happens to them when MySQL restarts?
option1: Only in RAM, so every index is rebuilt from the table each time MySQL starts
option2: On disk; pages in use are cached in RAM, and nothing is rebuilt on restart
option3: In a separate file that is deleted on shutdown and recreated on the next query
option4: Inside the application server, which sends the index to MySQL with every query
correctOptionExplanation: An index is stored data. Restarting only empties the cache; the trees on disk are still there.

questionText: An API pages through orders with ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 500000. What is the problem, and the usual fix?
option1: There is no problem: OFFSET makes the index jump directly to entry 500,001
option2: OFFSET cannot be used on indexed columns; remove the primary key from the table
option3: It walks past 500,000 entries only to drop them; use WHERE id < last_seen_id
option4: Add an index on OFFSET, so that MySQL can find the page number directly
correctOptionExplanation: OFFSET counts entries one by one. Remembering the last id seen lets the index jump straight to the next page.

questionText: EXPLAIN shows type = ALL and key = NULL. What does that tell you?
option1: The query used all indexes on the table at the same time
option2: A full table scan: no index was used, and every row is being read
option3: The query returned all rows, which is why no key was needed
option4: The best possible plan: the primary key was used for every row
correctOptionExplanation: ALL means "read the whole table". Look at the WHERE clause for a missing index, a function on the column, or a type mismatch.

questionText: EXPLAIN shows type = ref, key = idx_email, rows = 1. What does that tell you?
option1: MySQL looked the value up in idx_email and expects about one matching row
option2: MySQL scanned idx_email from start to end and kept the first row it found
option3: The query referenced another table, so MySQL used a join on email
option4: idx_email exists but was rejected, and one row was read from the table instead
correctOptionExplanation: ref = an index lookup on a value; key = the index chosen; rows = how many rows MySQL expects to examine.

questionText: EXPLAIN shows "Using filesort" for SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at. What does it mean, and what could help?
option1: MySQL sorts the rows itself; an index on (user_id, created_at) would avoid it
option2: The results are being written to a file on disk, so the server is running out of memory
option3: The query is broken and the ORDER BY clause is being ignored
option4: MySQL used the best possible plan, and nothing can be improved
correctOptionExplanation: filesort means an extra sorting step (not always on disk). An index that matches both the filter and the ORDER BY removes it.

questionText: EXPLAIN shows "Using index" in the Extra column. What does it mean?
option1: An index was used to find the rows, which then had to be read from the table
option2: MySQL created a temporary index just for this query
option3: The query was answered from the index alone (a covering index)
option4: The query used the primary key, which is the only index that can show this
correctOptionExplanation: Using index = covering index. It is the best case for a secondary index, because the second lookup is skipped.

questionText: EXPLAIN shows type = range, key = idx_created_at for WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-02-01'. What happened?
option1: MySQL read the entire index, because ranges always need a full index scan
option2: MySQL used a hash lookup for each day of January separately
option3: It jumped to the first January entry and read on in order until February
option4: MySQL scanned the table, and range only describes the dates being compared
correctOptionExplanation: range = a continuous stretch of the index. This is what a B+ tree is good at: jump to the start, then follow the linked leaves.

questionText: Index idx_city_age on students(city, age). Select ALL the queries that can use it to jump in.
option1: WHERE city = 'Pune'
option2: WHERE city = 'Pune' AND age = 30
option3: WHERE age = 30
option4: WHERE age = 30 AND city = 'Pune'
correctOptionExplanation: Any query that gives city can use the index; the order of conditions in WHERE does not matter. Age alone and a leading % give MySQL nowhere to jump in.

questionText: orders has an index on created_at. Select ALL the conditions that stop MySQL from using it to jump in.
option1: WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025
option2: WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01'
option3: WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2025-05-01'
option4: WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2025-05-01' AND '2025-05-31'
correctOptionExplanation: Any function or calculation on the indexed column hides it from the index. Keep the column bare and put the logic on the other side.

questionText: Select ALL the columns that are good candidates for an index.
option1: A column in the WHERE clause of a frequent query that matches only a few rows
option2: A foreign key column used to join two large tables
option3: A boolean column where 95% of rows have the same value
option4: The ORDER BY column of a hot query that returns only the top 20 rows
option5: A column that no query ever filters, joins or sorts on
correctOptionExplanation: Index what your queries search, join and sort by, especially when few rows match. Low-selectivity and unused columns only add write cost.

questionText: Select ALL the true statements about secondary (non-clustered) indexes in InnoDB.
option1: Each leaf holds the indexed value plus the primary key of the row
option2: Fetching columns that are not in the index needs a second trip into the primary key tree
option3: A table can have many secondary indexes
option4: They store a full copy of each row, just like the clustered index
option5: Creating one changes the physical order of the rows in the table
correctOptionExplanation: The table stays in primary key order; secondary indexes are extra sorted trees that point back to it through the primary key.

questionText: Select ALL the real costs of adding more indexes to a table.
option1: Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE has more trees to keep up to date
option2: More disk space is used
option3: More memory is needed to keep the useful index pages cached
option4: Queries that use the new index become slower
option5: The table can no longer have a primary key
correctOptionExplanation: Indexes speed up the reads they serve and cost on every write, on disk and in the buffer pool. Add them for real queries, not just in case.

questionText: Select ALL the situations where a full table scan is a reasonable plan.
option1: The table is tiny, such as 30 countries
option2: The query matches most of the rows in the table
option3: A nightly report has to read every row anyway
option4: Finding one user by email in a table of 10 million users
option5: Fetching one order by its primary key
correctOptionExplanation: A scan is not always bad. It is the right plan when the table is small or most rows are needed; it is a problem when you want a few rows out of millions.
